arc_intro: One day before the audit. Five layers secured, the mystery solved, new trust built correctly. Ravi has one last ask: make sure nothing at the outer perimeter can quietly slip again — not just today, but structurally, even if someone forgets everything you just spent this whole investigation learning.

tasks.scenario: Ravi opens the final meeting: 'Everything we found traces back to human habits — rushed setup, forgotten offboarding, sloppy policies. Tomorrow the auditor won't just check individual configs, they'll check whether we have real guardrails that hold even when a human forgets something. What's missing?'
tasks.question: What category of protection has this entire investigation NOT covered yet?
options: A) More detailed IAM policies — you've already covered this extensively

B) Guardrails that don't depend on any individual remembering to do the right thing — root account protection (MFA), account-wide enforcement (password policy), and organization-level rules that override even a mistake (SCPs)
C) Nothing is missing, the investigation is already complete
D) Better documentation of the existing IAM policies
tasks.explanation: Correct answer: Guardrails that don't depend on any individual remembering to do the right thing — root account protection (MFA), account-wide enforcement (password policy), and organization-level rules that override even a mistake (SCPs)
tasks.ren_correct: Exactly — this whole investigation has been about habits failing. Today is about protections that don't rely on habits at all.
tasks.ren_wrong: Not quite — revisit the core idea: who can do what, and can we prove it?

tasks.question: Root account MFA is enabled. If the root password gets phished tomorrow, what can the attacker do with just the password?
options: A) Log in immediately and take full control
B) Nothing — login is blocked without the live code from the registered MFA device
C) Log in with read-only access
D) Log in if they also know the account email
tasks.explanation: MFA, password only. Registered device- live code is needed.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — this is the single highest-leverage protection in the whole account.
tasks.ren_wrong: Not quite. MFA password only — device code.

tasks.scenario: You message ananya-analyst directly and walk her through MFA setup. She apologizes: 'I meant to do this weeks ago, just never got around to it.'
tasks.question: Why does her exact phrase — 'meant to do it, never got around to it' — matter more today than it would have at the start of this investigation?
expected_answer_contains: This is the exact same pattern that caused every major finding in this investigation — a task that was intended to happen but was deferred indefinitely
The fix here is small and low-stakes, but it's the same root cause as Vikram's 8-month-old permission, just caught immediately instead of months later
This is why moving to structural, automatic enforcement (rather than relying on individual follow-through) matters
tasks.explanation: 'Meant to do it, never got around to it' — This is Vikram case- exact echo, small scale-, immediately caught. pattern, different size — structural guardrails.

tasks.scenario: priya-dev has AdministratorAccess. She tries to create an S3 bucket in eu-west-1 for a quick European expansion test. The request fails.
tasks.error_shown: An error occurred (AccessDenied) when calling the CreateBucket operation: User: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/priya-dev is not authorized to perform: s3:CreateBucket on resource: "arn:aws:s3:::foodquick-eu-test" with an explicit deny in a service control policy
tasks.diagnosis: priya-dev's AdministratorAccess IAM policy technically allows this action. But the SCP on the Production OU denies all actions outside ap-south-1 — and that Deny is at the organization level, which overrides even AdministratorAccess entirely.
tasks.fix: Two valid paths: if this is a genuine approved expansion, update the SCP to allow eu-west-1 specifically. If it was just a quick test, create the bucket in the Sandbox OU instead, which doesn't carry this restriction.
tasks.explanation: Apply least privilege and keep a clear audit trail — that is the FoodQuick standard for FQ-142.

tasks.scenario: A new intern joins FoodQuick next week for a 2-month internship, zero prior AWS experience.
tasks.question: Which OU should their account go in, and why does this matter more given what you now know about Vikram's case?
options: A) Production OU — simpler to manage one environment
B) Sandbox OU — its SCP prevents any access to production resources structurally, regardless of what IAM permissions accidentally get granted or forgotten later
C) Development OU, since interns are part of the dev process
D) No OU needed, just limit their IAM permissions carefully
tasks.explanation: Sandbox OU- SCP structural protection. Vikram case- — IAM permission only, forget. Sandbox OU-, forget production touch do.
tasks.ren_correct: Right — and now you can explain exactly WHY, with a real example behind you.
tasks.ren_wrong: Not quite. IAM only — Sandbox OU structural safety, IAM permission forget.

tasks.scenario: An IAM policy explicitly Allows an action. An SCP explicitly Denies the same action, account-wide, as a temporary freeze during a company event.
tasks.question: What happens, and why do companies specifically use SCPs (not individual IAM policy edits) for temporary freezes like this?
expected_answer_contains: The action is denied — SCP Deny always overrides IAM Allow with no exceptions
A single SCP change enforces the freeze instantly across every user in the account, without needing to edit each person's individual IAM policy one at a time
When the freeze ends, removing the SCP restores normal behavior immediately for everyone at once
tasks.explanation: SCP Deny always IAM Allow-. SCP change, entire account- instantly enforce — 13 users- policies edit do.

tasks.scenario: Ravi asks the real closing question: 'If we'd had this Organizations and SCP setup BEFORE Vikram left, would any of this have been prevented?' Design the guardrail that answers this properly.

cases.case_1: Prevent any IAM user from ever creating a new IAM user with AdministratorAccess attached, account-wide, regardless of what their own IAM policy allows.
cases.case_2: Guarantee no account in the organization can ever disable CloudTrail logging, regardless of who has AdministratorAccess.
cases.case_3: Give the finance team visibility into aggregated billing across all accounts without any operational access to any of them.

correct_answers.case_1: An SCP denying iam:CreateUser combined with iam:AttachUserPolicy for AdministratorAccess specifically — this would have made it structurally impossible for Vikram's leftover permission to ever be used to create a new admin backdoor, even during the 14-day offboarding gap, even if the IAM permission itself was never revoked in time.
correct_answers.case_2: An SCP at the org root denying cloudtrail:StopLogging and cloudtrail:DeleteTrail — unbypassable even by AdministratorAccess.
correct_answers.case_3: AWS Organizations consolidated billing plus an IAM role scoped only to billing data, no operational permissions — visibility without operational risk.

tasks.explanation: Case 1 real answer to Ravi- question. IAM permission revoke do, SCP, Vikram- use do backdoor create do. session.

tasks.question: Why is the SCP from T8 (Case 1) a stronger fix than simply being more careful about removing permissions during offboarding?
options: A) It isn't stronger, both approaches are equally reliable
B) The SCP works even when a human forgets — it doesn't depend on anyone remembering to act correctly during a rushed or delayed offboarding, which is exactly what failed with Vikram
C) The SCP is only a backup and IAM cleanup is still the real fix
D) SCPs are easier to configure than IAM policies, that's the only advantage
tasks.explanation: Correct answer: The SCP works even when a human forgets — it doesn't depend on anyone remembering to act correctly during a rushed or delayed offboarding, which is exactly what failed with Vikram
tasks.ren_correct: This is the whole investigation's lesson in one sentence.
tasks.ren_wrong: Not quite — revisit the core idea: who can do what, and can we prove it?

tasks.scenario: The audit is tomorrow. FQ-142 is ready to close. Write the final report — not just this piece, but a short retrospective on the whole investigation.
tasks.question: Summarize: what FQ-142 actually was, what you found, and the one structural change that will outlast everyone's memory of this specific incident.
expected_answer_contains: Started as a routine 'clean up shared logins' request and became a full investigation tracing back to one former contractor's incomplete offboarding, 8 months of forgotten permissions
Every layer secured: Identity, Service Trust, Access Precision, Access Hygiene, Service Integration, and now Perimeter Defense
The single most important lasting change is the new SCP guardrail — because it protects the account even when, inevitably, someone eventually forgets something again
tasks.explanation: FQ-142. Simple ticket-, real investigation-, structural fix-. real cloud engineering — individual fires Not quite —, doing.

arc_outro: Perimeter Defense Layer: secured. FQ-142 — Secure IAM before audit — is officially resolved. Ravi reads the full retrospective and doesn't say much at first. 'Six weeks ago this was a two-line ticket about shared passwords. You turned it into the reason we'll actually pass tomorrow.' The audit happens the next morning. FoodQuick passes clean. Ravi's next message arrives before lunch: 'Networking's a mess too. You up for FQ-156?'
